subject: music
title: American folk revival (c. 1958–1965): acoustic guitars, protest songs, and the Greenwich Village coffeehouse that launched Dylan
dek: In November 1958 the Kingston Trio's 'Tom Dooley' reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100, and the folk revival was suddenly commercial. By 1959 Joan Baez was singing at the Newport Folk Festival. Bob Dylan arrived in New York in January 1961 and played Greenwich Village coffeehouses—Gerde's Folk City, the Gaslight, Café Wha?—where Dave Van Ronk, Odetta, and Phil Ochs were building a scene. The revival linked folk music to the civil rights movement: 'We Shall Overcome' at the 1963 March on Washington, the Freedom Singers touring the South. In July 1965 Dylan plugged in an electric guitar at Newport and the acoustic folk moment ended, splitting into folk rock (the Byrds, Simon & Garfunkel) and a purist backlash. What survived was the singer-songwriter as political voice.
honesty: Folk revival-era photographs from 1958–1965—club interiors, Newport Festival performances, civil rights marches with folk singers—are mostly in commercial archives, private collections, or controlled by estates under copyright. Iconic images of Bob Dylan at Newport 1965, Joan Baez at the March on Washington, or the Greenwich Village club scene are not freely licensed. This lesson proceeds text-only. All YouTube links point to official or Topic uploads; when official audio is unavailable the note explains what the link is. No AI images. No invented facts, quotes, dates, or chart positions.

timeline.label: The first folk wave: the Weavers, Harry Smith's Anthology, and the blacklist
timeline.detail: In the 1940s the Almanac Singers (Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger, Lee Hays) sang union songs and anti-fascist ballads. After World War II the Weavers—Pete Seeger, Lee Hays, Ronnie Gilbert, Fred Hellerman—formed in 1948 and had a number-one hit with Lead Belly's 'Goodnight Irene' in 1950. The Weavers played nightclubs and concert halls, bringing folk music to a mainstream audience. Then the blacklist arrived. In 1952, during the McCarthy era, Pete Seeger and the Weavers were blacklisted for alleged Communist ties. The group disbanded in 1952, reunited for a Carnegie Hall concert in 1955, but their commercial moment was over. In 1952 Folkways Records released Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music, a six-LP collection of commercial 78 rpm recordings from 1927–1932: Appalachian ballads, blues, gospel, Cajun. The Anthology became a sacred text for the next generation of folk revivalists. Sing Out! magazine, founded in 1950 by Pete Seeger and others, became the folk community's journal.

timeline.label: The Kingston Trio's 'Tom Dooley' reaches number one
timeline.detail: The Kingston Trio—Bob Shane, Nick Reynolds, Dave Guard—were clean-cut college students from the San Francisco Bay Area who sang Appalachian ballads and calypso songs in a smooth, commercial style. In June 1958 Capitol Records released their version of 'Tom Dooley,' a traditional North Carolina murder ballad. By November 1958 the single reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and stayed on the charts for five months. The Kingston Trio's self-titled album spent four weeks at number one on the album chart. 'Tom Dooley' sold over three million copies. The folk revival was suddenly profitable. Record labels began signing folk acts. College students bought acoustic guitars. Coffeehouses and folk clubs opened in cities across the US.

timeline.label: Joan Baez at the first Newport Folk Festival
timeline.detail: The Newport Folk Festival, organized by George Wein, debuted in July 1959 in Newport, Rhode Island. Joan Baez, an eighteen-year-old soprano from New York, performed and captivated the audience. Baez sang traditional ballads in a clear, unaccompanied voice, with minimal guitar. She had been singing at Club 47 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and coffeehouses in Boston. After Newport, Baez became the face of the folk revival's serious, purist wing: no commercialism, no pop arrangements, just voice and guitar. Her debut album, Joan Baez (Vanguard, 1960), reached number three on the Billboard album chart and stayed on the chart for over two years. By 1962 she was on the cover of Time magazine.

timeline.label: Bob Dylan arrives in New York; Greenwich Village scene
timeline.detail: In January 1961 Bob Dylan (born Robert Zimmerman in Duluth, Minnesota) arrived in New York City at age nineteen. He came to visit Woody Guthrie, who was hospitalized with Huntington's disease. Dylan began performing at Greenwich Village coffeehouses: Gerde's Folk City, the Gaslight Cafe, Cafe Wha?, the Bitter End. The Village folk scene was dense: Dave Van Ronk (a blues and jug-band specialist who became Dylan's mentor), Odetta (a gospel-trained singer with a powerful voice), Ramblin' Jack Elliott (a Woody Guthrie disciple), the New Lost City Ramblers (old-time string-band revivalists), and dozens of young singers playing for tips. Dylan absorbed the repertoire—traditional ballads, Guthrie's Dust Bowl songs, blues—and began writing his own topical songs. In September 1961 New York Times critic Robert Shelton reviewed Dylan's performance at Gerde's Folk City, calling him 'one of the most compelling young folk singers to be heard in many a moon.' John Hammond of Columbia Records signed Dylan shortly after.

timeline.label: Dylan's first album; Broadside magazine; the rediscovered blues singers
timeline.detail: Bob Dylan's self-titled debut (Columbia, March 1962) sold poorly—only about 5,000 copies in its first year. The album was mostly traditional songs and covers, with only two originals. Dylan was called 'Hammond's Folly' inside Columbia. But Dylan was writing prolifically. Broadside magazine, founded in February 1962 by Agnes 'Sis' Cunningham, Gordon Friesen, and Gil Turner, published topical songs in mimeographed form. Dylan contributed 'Blowin' in the Wind,' 'A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall,' and others to Broadside before recording them. Meanwhile, older blues singers—Mississippi John Hurt, Son House, Skip James—were 'rediscovered' by young white folk enthusiasts who had heard their 1920s recordings on Harry Smith's Anthology. These men, some in their sixties and seventies, were brought to Newport and other festivals and recorded for Vanguard, Prestige, and other labels. The folk revival was recovering a Black rural tradition and, awkwardly, profiting from it.

timeline.label: The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan and 'Blowin' in the Wind'
timeline.detail: In May 1963 Columbia released The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, Dylan's second album. The album included 'Blowin' in the Wind,' 'A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall,' 'Masters of War,' 'Don't Think Twice, It's All Right,' and 'Girl from the North Country.' These were original songs, not traditional covers. 'Blowin' in the Wind'—with its rhetorical questions about war, freedom, and peace—became the folk revival's anthem. Peter, Paul and Mary's cover of 'Blowin' in the Wind' (released June 1963) reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and sold over one million copies. Dylan became the voice of a generation, though he resisted the label. The album reached number 22 on the Billboard album chart and stayed on the chart for nearly two years.

timeline.label: March on Washington and 'We Shall Overcome'
timeline.detail: On 28 August 1963 the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom drew over 250,000 people to the National Mall in Washington, D.C. Folk singers were central to the day. Joan Baez sang 'We Shall Overcome,' the civil rights anthem adapted from a gospel hymn and popularized by Pete Seeger, Guy Carawan, and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). Peter, Paul and Mary performed 'If I Had a Hammer' and 'Blowin' in the Wind.' Bob Dylan sang 'When the Ship Comes In.' Odetta, Mahalia Jackson, and the Freedom Singers (a group of SNCC activists who sang at sit-ins and marches) also performed. The folk revival and the civil rights movement were intertwined: SNCC field organizers taught 'We Shall Overcome' and 'Keep Your Eyes on the Prize' to activists in the South; Northern folk singers raised funds and awareness. The March on Washington was the folk revival's public peak.

timeline.label: The Times They Are A-Changin' and the protest-song moment
timeline.detail: In January 1964 Dylan released The Times They Are A-Changin', an album of protest and topical songs. The title track became an anthem of generational change. Other songwriters were writing in the same vein: Phil Ochs ('I Ain't Marching Anymore,' 'Draft Dodger Rag'), Tom Paxton ('The Last Thing on My Mind'), Buffy Sainte-Marie ('Universal Soldier'), Malvina Reynolds ('Little Boxes'). Judy Collins, a classically trained singer from Colorado, recorded albums of Dylan songs and traditional ballads. Ian & Sylvia, a Canadian duo, sang traditional and contemporary folk. The Hootenanny TV show, which aired on ABC from 1963 to 1964, brought folk music to living rooms nationwide, though the show blacklisted Pete Seeger and refused to let him appear. The folk revival was commercial and political at once, a tension that could not hold.

timeline.label: Dylan moves beyond protest; Bringing It All Back Home
timeline.detail: By 1964 Dylan was tiring of the protest-song label. In August 1964 he released Another Side of Bob Dylan, which included personal and surreal songs ('My Back Pages,' 'Chimes of Freedom') rather than topical anthems. In March 1965 he released Bringing It All Back Home, which featured electric instruments on side one—rock band, electric guitar, organ—and acoustic songs on side two. 'Subterranean Homesick Blues' was a rock single with a promotional film (an early music video). Dylan was moving toward rock, influenced by the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, and the British Invasion. Folk purists were alarmed. Dylan was supposed to be the voice of authenticity, not a pop star.

timeline.label: Newport Folk Festival: Dylan goes electric
timeline.detail: On 25 July 1965 Bob Dylan performed at the Newport Folk Festival with an electric rock band: Mike Bloomfield on guitar, Al Kooper on organ, Jerome Arnold on bass, Sam Lay on drums. Dylan played three songs—'Maggie's Farm,' 'Like a Rolling Stone,' and 'It Takes a Lot to Laugh, It Takes a Train to Cry'—and was met with boos and shouts from parts of the audience. (Some booed the poor sound quality; others booed the electric instruments; the details are disputed.) Pete Seeger was reportedly upset, though accounts vary. Dylan left the stage after three electric songs, returned with an acoustic guitar, and played 'Mr. Tambourine Man' and 'It's All Over Now, Baby Blue.' The moment became mythic: the folk revival's end, the birth of folk rock, Dylan's rejection of the protest-song mantle. Whether Dylan was actually booed or whether the reaction was overstated, the symbolic break was real.

timeline.label: Folk rock: the Byrds, Simon & Garfunkel, and the electric split
timeline.detail: In April 1965 the Byrds released 'Mr. Tambourine Man,' a rock arrangement of Dylan's song with twelve-string electric guitars, harmonies, and a driving beat. The single reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. In September 1965 Dylan released Highway 61 Revisited, a full electric rock album with 'Like a Rolling Stone,' which reached number two. In October 1965 Simon & Garfunkel's 'The Sound of Silence' was overdubbed with electric instruments by producer Tom Wilson without the duo's knowledge and re-released; it reached number one in January 1966. Folk rock was a commercial genre: electric instruments, rock rhythms, folk melodies, and introspective lyrics. The Mamas & the Papas, the Lovin' Spoonful, and Donovan followed. The acoustic folk revival was over, split between those who went electric and those who retreated to the purist folk scene.

listen.title: The Kingston Trio — Tom Dooley (1958)
listen.note: Capitol Records, 1958. Traditional North Carolina murder ballad arranged by the Kingston Trio. Reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in November 1958 and launched the folk revival boom. Sold over three million copies.

listen.title: The Weavers — Goodnight Irene (1950)
listen.note: Decca Records, 1950. Lead Belly's song arranged by the Weavers. Reached number one in 1950. The Weavers were blacklisted in 1952 during the McCarthy era, ending the first folk wave.

listen.title: Joan Baez — Silver Dagger (1960)
listen.note: Vanguard Records, 1960. Traditional ballad from Joan Baez's debut album. Baez's clear soprano and minimal guitar defined the folk revival's purist wing.

listen.title: Bob Dylan — Blowin' in the Wind (1963)
listen.note: Columbia Records, 1963. From The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan. Became the folk revival's anthem. Peter, Paul and Mary's cover reached number two on the Hot 100.

listen.title: Peter, Paul and Mary — If I Had a Hammer (1962)
listen.note: Warner Bros., 1962. Written by Pete Seeger and Lee Hays in 1949. Reached number ten on the Hot 100. Peter, Paul and Mary were the folk revival's most commercially successful group.

listen.title: Pete Seeger — We Shall Overcome (1963)
listen.note: Columbia Records, 1963. Civil rights anthem adapted from a gospel hymn. Pete Seeger and Guy Carawan taught it to SNCC activists. Joan Baez sang it at the March on Washington.

listen.title: Bob Dylan — The Times They Are A-Changin' (1964)
listen.note: Columbia Records, 1964. Dylan's anthem of generational and political change. Title track from his January 1964 album.

listen.title: Phil Ochs — I Ain't Marching Anymore (1965)
listen.note: Elektra Records, 1965. Anti-war protest song by one of the folk revival's most committed topical songwriters. Ochs remained in the acoustic protest-song tradition after Dylan moved on.

listen.title: The Byrds — Mr. Tambourine Man (1965)
listen.note: Columbia Records, 1965. Dylan's song arranged as folk rock with twelve-string electric guitars and harmonies. Reached number one on the Hot 100. Marked the birth of folk rock.

listen.title: Bob Dylan — Like a Rolling Stone (1965)
listen.note: Columbia Records, 1965. Six-minute electric rock single from Highway 61 Revisited. Reached number two on the Hot 100. Dylan had fully moved to electric rock.

fun_fact.title: Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music was sourced from one man's obsessive 78 rpm record collection
fun_fact.text: In 1952 Folkways Records released Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music, a six-LP set of eighty-four tracks recorded between 1927 and 1932. Harry Smith (1923–1991) was an experimental filmmaker, painter, and record collector who had amassed thousands of 78 rpm records, buying them from junk shops and estate sales. Smith selected eighty-four tracks—Appalachian ballads, blues, gospel, Cajun music—and organized them thematically rather than chronologically or by genre. The Anthology included Clarence Ashley's 'The Coo Coo Bird,' the Carter Family's 'Engine 143,' Mississippi John Hurt's 'Frankie,' Blind Lemon Jefferson's 'See That My Grave Is Kept Clean,' and Bascom Lamar Lunsford's 'I Wish I Was a Mole in the Ground.' The booklet included Smith's eccentric liner notes and illustrations. The Anthology became a sacred text for the 1950s and 1960s folk revival. Bob Dylan, Joan Baez, Dave Van Ronk, and others learned songs from it. In 1991, shortly before Smith's death, the Anthology was reissued on CD, and in 1997 it was added to the National Recording Registry of the Library of Congress. Smith's collection, sourced from one man's obsessive crate-digging, became the foundation of the American folk canon.

sections.title: The first folk wave: Woody Guthrie, the Weavers, and the blacklist that ended it

blocks.text: In the 1940s, during the Great Depression and World War II, American folk music was already political. Woody Guthrie, an Oklahoma-born singer and songwriter, traveled the country playing union halls, migrant camps, and radical gatherings. His songs—'This Land Is Your Land,' 'I Ain't Got No Home,' 'Deportee (Plane Wreck at Los Gatos)'—documented the Dust Bowl, labor struggles, and the lives of working people. Guthrie's guitar famously bore the slogan 'This machine kills fascists.' He was not a trained musician; he was a storyteller who used traditional melodies and plain language. Guthrie sang with the Almanac Singers, a loose collective that included Pete Seeger and Lee Hays, performing at strikes and rallies. The Almanac Singers sang anti-fascist songs after the US entered World War II, but they disbanded in 1943.

After the war, Pete Seeger, Lee Hays, Ronnie Gilbert, and Fred Hellerman formed the Weavers in 1948. The Weavers were more polished than the Almanac Singers: four-part harmonies, arrangements suitable for nightclubs and concert halls. They signed with Decca Records and recorded Lead Belly's 'Goodnight Irene' with orchestral accompaniment. The single reached number one on the Billboard chart in 1950 and stayed there for thirteen weeks. It sold over two million copies. The Weavers appeared on television and played the top venues. Folk music, for a brief moment, was commercially viable.

Then the blacklist arrived. In 1950 the pamphlet Red Channels accused 151 entertainers of Communist sympathies or associations. Pete Seeger and the Weavers were listed. In 1952, during the McCarthy era, Seeger was blacklisted. The Weavers' bookings dried up. Decca dropped them. Television and radio refused to play their records. The group disbanded in 1952. They reunited for a sold-out Carnegie Hall concert on Christmas Eve 1955, which was recorded and released as an album, but the commercial moment was over. Pete Seeger would spend the next decade fighting the blacklist, eventually being cited for contempt of Congress in 1957 for refusing to answer questions before the House Un-American Activities Committee. His conviction was overturned on appeal in 1962.

In 1952, the same year the Weavers disbanded, Folkways Records released Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music. Smith, an experimental filmmaker and obsessive record collector, had compiled eighty-four tracks from commercial 78 rpm recordings made between 1927 and 1932. The six-LP set included Appalachian ballads, blues, gospel, Cajun songs, and old-time string-band music. Smith organized the tracks thematically—Ballads, Social Music, Songs—rather than by artist or chronology. The Anthology included no contemporary recordings; it was an archive, a time capsule. The accompanying booklet featured Smith's eccentric liner notes and hand-drawn illustrations. The Anthology was expensive and obscure, sold mostly through Folkways' mail-order catalog, but it became a sacred text. A generation of young folk enthusiasts—Bob Dylan, Joan Baez, Dave Van Ronk—learned songs from it. The Anthology created a canon.

sections.title: November 1958: the Kingston Trio's 'Tom Dooley' and the boom begins

blocks.text: The Kingston Trio were not radicals. Bob Shane, Nick Reynolds, and Dave Guard were clean-cut college students from the San Francisco Bay Area. They sang traditional folk songs—Appalachian ballads, calypso, sea shanties—in smooth three-part harmonies with strummed acoustic guitars. Their repertoire came from Alan Lomax's field recordings and folk-song collections, but their presentation was collegiate, polished, and apolitical. They wore matching striped shirts. They smiled. They looked like fraternity brothers, which some of them had been.

In June 1958 Capitol Records released the Kingston Trio's version of 'Tom Dooley,' a traditional North Carolina murder ballad about a man named Tom Dula who was hanged in 1868 for killing his lover Laura Foster. The song had been collected by folklorist Frank Warner in the 1930s and 1940s. The Kingston Trio's arrangement was simple: three voices, three guitars, no drums, no bass. The lyric was mournful but the delivery was smooth. 'Tom Dooley' was released as a single in June 1958. By November it had reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100, where it stayed for a week. The single sold over three million copies. The Kingston Trio's self-titled album, released in 1958, spent four weeks at number one on the album chart and remained on the chart for nearly four years.

'Tom Dooley' made folk music profitable. Record labels began signing folk acts. College students, especially at elite universities, bought acoustic guitars and formed folk groups. Coffeehouses opened in cities across the United States, providing stages for singers. Folk music became associated with college-educated, middle-class young people, which was a shift from its earlier association with labor organizers and rural singers. The Kingston Trio's success created a commercial infrastructure: record contracts, booking agents, college concert circuits, folk festivals. By 1959 folk music was a growth industry.

But the Kingston Trio were not universally admired. To purists—those who had followed the Weavers, who listened to Folkways Records, who knew Lead Belly and Woody Guthrie—the Kingston Trio were too slick, too commercial, too disconnected from the music's roots. The Kingston Trio did not write songs; they arranged traditional material. They did not play blues or old-time banjo styles; they strummed chords. They did not sing about labor or injustice; they sang ballads. This tension—between commercial folk and authentic folk, between entertainment and politics, between the middle class and the working class—would define the revival.

sections.title: Greenwich Village coffeehouses: where Dylan learned from Dave Van Ronk and Odetta

blocks.text: In January 1961 Bob Dylan, nineteen years old, arrived in New York City from Minneapolis. He had been born Robert Zimmerman in Duluth, Minnesota, and had adopted the name Dylan after reading Dylan Thomas (though he later denied this). Dylan came to New York to visit Woody Guthrie, who was hospitalized at Greystone Park Psychiatric Hospital in New Jersey with Huntington's disease. Dylan visited Guthrie regularly, playing him songs and learning from him. But Dylan's real education happened in Greenwich Village, the neighborhood in lower Manhattan where folk singers congregated.

The Village folk scene was centered in coffeehouses: Gerde's Folk City on West 4th Street, the Gaslight Cafe on MacDougal Street, Cafe Wha? (also on MacDougal), and the Bitter End. These were small rooms with low ceilings, espresso machines, and a stage or a corner where singers performed. The pay was minimal—tips, a passed hat, maybe five dollars a night—but the scene was dense. On any night you might hear Dave Van Ronk, a bearded blues singer with a gravelly voice who played ragtime guitar and Lead Belly covers; Odetta, a classically trained contralto with a powerful, gospel-inflected delivery; Ramblin' Jack Elliott, who had traveled with Woody Guthrie and sang in Guthrie's style; the New Lost City Ramblers, a string band that played old-time Appalachian music with banjo, fiddle, and guitar; and dozens of younger singers learning the repertoire.

Dave Van Ronk became Dylan's mentor. Van Ronk was ten years older and knew the Village. He taught Dylan blues arrangements, guitar tunings, and how to navigate the scene. Van Ronk's apartment on Waverly Place was a gathering place where singers swapped songs and drank cheap wine. Dylan absorbed everything: traditional ballads from the Harry Smith Anthology, Guthrie's talking blues style, blues from Mississippi John Hurt and Blind Lemon Jefferson, Irish ballads, Scottish ballads, Carter Family songs. Dylan was a sponge. He learned a song after hearing it once. He borrowed Van Ronk's arrangement of 'House of the Rising Sun' without asking (Van Ronk was annoyed but accepted it). Dylan played harmonica in a rack around his neck and sang in a nasal, reedy voice that some found grating and others found riveting.

In September 1961 New York Times critic Robert Shelton attended a show at Gerde's Folk City where Dylan was opening for the Greenbriar Boys, a bluegrass band. Shelton's review, published on September 29, called Dylan 'one of the most compelling young folk singers to be heard in many a moon.' Shelton praised Dylan's voice—'raucous and highly effective'—and his songwriting. The review changed Dylan's career. John Hammond, a legendary Columbia Records producer who had signed Billie Holiday, Count Basie, and Aretha Franklin, read the review and came to see Dylan. Hammond signed Dylan to Columbia in October 1961.

Dylan's self-titled debut album, released in March 1962, sold poorly—about 5,000 copies in its first year. The album was mostly traditional songs and covers: 'House of the Rising Sun' (Van Ronk's arrangement), 'Man of Constant Sorrow,' Blind Lemon Jefferson's 'See That My Grave Is Kept Clean,' and two Dylan originals, 'Song to Woody' and 'Talkin' New York.' Columbia executives called Dylan 'Hammond's Folly.' But Dylan was writing constantly. By 1962 he had a notebook full of original songs, many of them topical: protests against war, racism, and injustice. These songs would appear on his second album and change the folk revival.

sections.title: 'We Shall Overcome': folk music and the civil rights movement

blocks.text: 'We Shall Overcome' began as a gospel hymn, 'I'll Overcome Someday,' written by Charles Albert Tindley and published in 1901. In the 1940s it was adapted by tobacco workers on strike in Charleston, South Carolina, who sang 'We will overcome' on the picket line. In 1947 Zilphia Horton, music director at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee, learned the song from the strikers and taught it to Pete Seeger. Seeger changed 'will' to 'shall' and added verses. In 1960 Guy Carawan, a folk singer and Highlander staff member, taught 'We Shall Overcome' to Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) activists at a workshop. SNCC adopted it as the movement's anthem.

The folk revival and the civil rights movement were intertwined. SNCC activists sang 'We Shall Overcome' at sit-ins, marches, and in jail cells. The Freedom Singers—Rutha Mae Harris, Bernice Johnson Reagon, Cordell Reagon, and Charles Neblett—were SNCC field organizers who formed a group to raise funds and awareness. They toured the North, singing at colleges and churches, and appeared at the 1963 Newport Folk Festival. Other songs became movement standards: 'Keep Your Eyes on the Prize' (adapted from the gospel hymn 'Keep Your Hand on the Plow'), 'Oh Freedom,' 'Ain't Gonna Let Nobody Turn Me Around,' 'We Shall Not Be Moved.' These were call-and-response songs, designed to be sung by a crowd, not by a soloist on a stage.

On August 28, 1963, over 250,000 people gathered at the National Mall in Washington, D.C., for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Folk singers were central to the program. Joan Baez opened the afternoon with 'Oh Freedom' and later sang 'We Shall Overcome.' Peter, Paul and Mary performed 'If I Had a Hammer' (written by Pete Seeger and Lee Hays) and 'Blowin' in the Wind' (Dylan's song, which Peter, Paul and Mary had recently taken to number two on the Billboard Hot 100). Bob Dylan sang 'When the Ship Comes In' and 'Only a Pawn in Their Game,' a song about the murder of Medgar Evers. Odetta sang, as did Mahalia Jackson, whose performance of 'I Been 'Buked and I Been Scorned' preceded Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech. The folk revival had become the soundtrack of the civil rights movement.

But the relationship was complicated. Most of the Northern folk singers were white. Most of the movement's activists and leaders were Black. White folk singers raised money, performed at rallies, and brought attention to the cause, but they did not face the same risks. Northern white college students could sing 'We Shall Overcome' at a hootenanny and go home; Black activists in Mississippi and Alabama sang it in jail after being beaten. Some activists welcomed the support; others resented the attention that white folk singers received. Bernice Johnson Reagon, one of the Freedom Singers, later said that 'We Shall Overcome' became 'a song that white people sang' at protests, while Black activists sang other songs that had not been adopted by the folk revival. The folk revival was borrowing from Black culture, again.

sections.title: The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan: original songs replace traditional covers

blocks.text: In May 1963 Columbia released The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, Dylan's second album. Where his debut had been mostly traditional songs and covers, Freewheelin' was almost entirely original compositions. The album included 'Blowin' in the Wind,' 'A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall,' 'Masters of War,' 'Don't Think Twice, It's All Right,' and 'Girl from the North Country.' These were not traditional folk songs; they were Dylan's songs, written in a folk idiom but with contemporary references and surreal imagery.

'Blowin' in the Wind,' with its series of rhetorical questions—'How many roads must a man walk down / Before you call him a man?'—became the folk revival's anthem. The lyric was broad enough to apply to war, civil rights, or any form of injustice. Peter, Paul and Mary's cover, released in June 1963, reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and sold over one million copies. It was the first Dylan song to become a pop hit. Dylan's original version, by contrast, was spare: voice, guitar, harmonica. The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan reached number 22 on the Billboard album chart and stayed on the chart for nearly two years. Dylan, at twenty-two, was the voice of a generation, though he resisted the label and later mocked it.

Other songwriters were writing in a similar mode. Phil Ochs, a journalism student turned singer, wrote topical songs that were more directly political than Dylan's: 'I Ain't Marching Anymore,' an anti-war anthem; 'Draft Dodger Rag,' a satirical song about evading military service; 'Love Me, I'm a Liberal,' which mocked moderate liberals. Tom Paxton wrote 'The Last Thing on My Mind,' a love song that became a folk standard, and 'Lyndon Johnson Told the Nation,' about the Vietnam War. Buffy Sainte-Marie, a Cree singer from Canada, wrote 'Universal Soldier,' an anti-war song that became an international hit when Donovan covered it. Judy Collins, a classically trained soprano from Colorado, recorded Dylan songs and traditional ballads, bringing a clear, operatic voice to the folk repertoire. These were singer-songwriters, not traditional folk singers. They wrote their own material, and their material was about the present, not the past.

sections.title: Newport: Dylan goes electric and the acoustic moment ends

blocks.text: By 1964 Dylan was tiring of the protest-song label. In August 1964 he released Another Side of Bob Dylan, an album of personal and surreal songs rather than topical anthems. In March 1965 he released Bringing It All Back Home, which featured electric instruments on side one—rock band, electric guitar, organ—and acoustic songs on side two. 'Subterranean Homesick Blues,' a rock single, was released with a promotional film (an early music video) directed by D. A. Pennebaker. Dylan was moving toward rock and roll, influenced by the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, and the British Invasion. Folk purists were alarmed.

On July 25, 1965, Bob Dylan performed at the Newport Folk Festival with an electric rock band. The band included Mike Bloomfield on guitar, Al Kooper on organ, Jerome Arnold on bass, and Sam Lay on drums. Dylan played three songs: 'Maggie's Farm,' 'Like a Rolling Stone,' and 'It Takes a Lot to Laugh, It Takes a Train to Cry.' The sound was loud, aggressive, and raw. Parts of the audience booed. Some accounts say they were booing the poor sound quality—the mixing was hasty and the vocals were buried—while others say they were booing the electric instruments. Pete Seeger was reportedly upset; some accounts claim he threatened to cut the sound cables with an axe, though Seeger later denied this. Dylan left the stage after three electric songs.

He returned with an acoustic guitar and played 'Mr. Tambourine Man' and 'It's All Over Now, Baby Blue' solo. The crowd cheered. Whether Dylan was actually booed or whether the reaction was exaggerated later, the moment became mythic. Newport 1965 is remembered as the end of the acoustic folk revival and the birth of folk rock, the moment when Dylan rejected the protest-song mantle and the folk purists rejected him. In reality the break was more gradual, but the symbolism was real. Dylan would not perform acoustically again for years.

In September 1965 Dylan released Highway 61 Revisited, a full electric rock album. The opening track, 'Like a Rolling Stone,' was six minutes long and reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100. The song was a rock anthem, not a folk song. Dylan's voice was the same—nasal, cutting—but the arrangement was loud, organ-driven, and relentless. The folk revival, in its acoustic, purist form, was over.

sections.title: Folk rock: the Byrds, Simon & Garfunkel, and the electric afterlife

blocks.text: In April 1965, three months before Newport, the Byrds released 'Mr. Tambourine Man,' a rock arrangement of Dylan's song. The Byrds were a Los Angeles band—Jim McGuinn (later Roger McGuinn), Gene Clark, David Crosby, Chris Hillman, Michael Clarke—who played twelve-string electric guitars, sang harmonies influenced by the Beatles, and used rock rhythms. 'Mr. Tambourine Man' reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. Folk rock was suddenly a commercial genre: electric instruments, rock rhythms, folk melodies, and introspective lyrics.

In October 1965 Simon & Garfunkel's 'The Sound of Silence' was overdubbed with electric instruments by producer Tom Wilson without Paul Simon or Art Garfunkel's knowledge. The duo had recorded the song acoustically for their 1964 album Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M., which had sold poorly. Wilson, who had also produced Dylan's Highway 61 Revisited, added electric guitar, bass, and drums to the acoustic track. The electric version was released as a single and reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1966. Simon & Garfunkel, who had broken up after their debut album flopped, reunited and recorded more folk rock albums.

Other acts followed: the Mamas & the Papas (folk harmonies with pop arrangements), the Lovin' Spoonful (jug-band folk with electric guitars), Donovan (a British Dylan imitator who moved to psychedelic folk rock), and the Turtles. Folk rock was mainstream. It was also, by 1966, no longer the folk revival. The acoustic coffeehouse scene continued—Phil Ochs, Tom Paxton, and others kept writing topical songs—but the commercial and cultural energy had moved to electric rock. The folk revival, as a distinct movement, lasted from 1958 to 1965. What survived was the singer-songwriter tradition: personal lyrics, social commentary, and the idea that a solo artist with a guitar could say something that mattered.

sections.title: Folk revivals in Britain, nueva canción in Latin America, and the global moment

blocks.text: The United States was not the only country experiencing a folk revival in the late 1950s and early 1960s. In Britain, a parallel movement emerged, centered on folk clubs in London, Manchester, and other cities. Ewan MacColl and A. L. Lloyd were the movement's elders: MacColl wrote 'The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face' and 'Dirty Old Town,' and Lloyd was a scholar of English folk songs. The British revival was more concerned with authenticity and preservation than the American revival. MacColl's Critics Group, a collective of singers, enforced strict rules: singers could only perform songs from their own regional or ethnic tradition. This meant English singers sang English songs, Scottish singers sang Scottish songs, and so on. Shirley Collins, Anne Briggs, and Martin Carthy were key figures in the British revival, singing traditional ballads with minimal accompaniment.

In January 1962 Bob Dylan visited London and played folk clubs, including the Troubadour and Bunjies. He met Martin Carthy, who taught him the traditional English ballad 'Scarborough Fair' (which Dylan adapted as 'Girl from the North Country') and 'Lord Franklin' (which became the melody for 'Bob Dylan's Dream'). British folk musicians were aware of the American revival, and vice versa, but the two movements had different priorities. The British revival was more invested in preserving traditional forms; the American revival, by the mid-1960s, was moving toward original songwriting and electric instruments.

Skiffle, a British genre that emerged in the mid-1950s, was a bridge between folk and rock. Skiffle bands played folk, blues, and American country songs with acoustic guitars, washboards, and homemade bass instruments. Lonnie Donegan's 'Rock Island Line' (1955) was a skiffle hit. The Beatles, before they were the Beatles, played skiffle. Skiffle introduced working-class British teenagers to American folk and blues, and many skiffle players later formed rock bands. Skiffle was a folk revival of sorts, but it was not concerned with authenticity or tradition—it was about accessibility and DIY energy.

In Latin America, nueva canción (new song) emerged in the 1960s as a parallel to the American and British folk revivals. Nueva canción was explicitly political: singers wrote songs about social justice, indigenous rights, and resistance to military dictatorships. Violeta Parra in Chile was a key figure: she collected traditional Chilean folk songs, recorded them, and wrote her own songs. Parra's 'Gracias a la Vida' (1966) became an anthem. Her children, Isabel and Angel Parra, continued her work. Víctor Jara, also Chilean, was a theater director, singer, and activist. His songs addressed land reform, worker rights, and political repression. Jara was murdered by the Chilean military in 1973 during the coup that brought Augusto Pinochet to power.

In Argentina, Atahualpa Yupanqui sang indigenous folk songs and wrote about rural life and social inequality. In Argentina and Uruguay, Mercedes Sosa, known as 'the voice of the voiceless Americas,' became the voice of nueva canción. Her 1963 manifesto, part of the Nuevo Cancionero movement, declared that folk music must address the present and serve the people. Nueva canción was folk music as resistance, connected to liberation theology, indigenous movements, and left-wing politics. It paralleled the American folk revival's connection to the civil rights movement, but it was more overtly revolutionary and faced more direct state repression.

sections.title: The singer-songwriter tradition and what the folk revival left behind

blocks.text: By 1966 the acoustic folk revival was over. Dylan had gone electric. The Byrds and Simon & Garfunkel were playing rock arrangements of folk songs. The civil rights movement had moved from marches to Black Power and urban uprisings, and 'We Shall Overcome' no longer seemed adequate. The Vietnam War was escalating, and the protest songs of 1963 felt quaint. The folk revival, as a commercial and cultural moment, lasted roughly from 1958 to 1965. But its legacy was durable.

The folk revival established the singer-songwriter as a legitimate artistic role. Before the revival, pop songs were mostly written by professional songwriters (the Brill Building, Motown's in-house teams) and performed by singers who did not write their own material. The folk revival normalized the idea that a performer could be the author, that personal experience and political conviction could be the source of a song. Joni Mitchell, Leonard Cohen, James Taylor, Carole King, and the entire 1970s singer-songwriter genre emerged from this tradition. The folk revival also created an audience that valued authenticity, sincerity, and lyrical depth over commercial polish. This audience would later support punk, indie rock, and alternative music.

The folk revival also demonstrated the commercial power of countercultural music. The Kingston Trio, Peter, Paul and Mary, and Bob Dylan sold millions of records while singing about injustice, war, and social change. Record labels learned that there was a market for music that challenged the status quo, as long as it was packaged well. This opened the door for the counterculture of the late 1960s—psychedelic rock, protest rock, and the idea that rock music could be art. The folk revival's infrastructure—the coffeehouse circuit, the festival model, the college concert tour—also survived and was adapted by later genres.

The folk revival's contradictions also persisted. It was a movement that celebrated authenticity while profiting from borrowed traditions. It was largely white and middle-class while drawing from Black and working-class sources. It claimed to be anti-commercial while producing best-selling albums and Top 40 hits. It championed the 'folk' while turning individual performers into stars. These contradictions were not resolved; they were inherited by the genres that followed. The folk revival's most lasting contribution may be the idea that popular music can be personal, political, and profitable at once.

If the American folk revival was powered by young, middle-class, college-educated white people who borrowed songs from Black blues singers, Appalachian balladeers, and rural traditions they did not belong to, who got to decide what counted as authentic? And if authenticity was the movement's central value, why did the most commercially successful acts—the Kingston Trio, Peter, Paul and Mary—sound the least like the sources they claimed to honor?

glossary.explain: American music movement c. 1958–1965 that revived interest in traditional folk songs, promoted singer-songwriters, and linked folk music to civil rights and anti-war activism.
Folk group (Bob Shane, Nick Reynolds, Dave Guard) whose 'Tom Dooley' (1958) reached number one and launched the folk revival boom.
Traditional North Carolina murder ballad; the Kingston Trio's 1958 version reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and sold over three million copies.
Singer-songwriter (born Robert Zimmerman, 1941) who arrived in New York in 1961, wrote 'Blowin' in the Wind' and 'The Times They Are A-Changin',' went electric at Newport 1965.
Singer (1941–) who performed at the first Newport Folk Festival (1959) and became the face of the folk revival's purist wing; sang at the 1963 March on Washington.
Singer, songwriter, and activist (1919–2014); member of the Weavers, blacklisted in 1952, wrote 'If I Had a Hammer,' taught 'We Shall Overcome' to civil rights activists.
Folk group (Pete Seeger, Lee Hays, Ronnie Gilbert, Fred Hellerman) who had a number-one hit with 'Goodnight Irene' (1950) and were blacklisted in 1952.
Singer-songwriter (1912–1967) who wrote 'This Land Is Your Land' and documented the Dust Bowl and labor struggles; Bob Dylan visited him in the hospital in 1961.
Neighborhood in lower Manhattan where the folk revival centered; coffeehouses included Gerde's Folk City, the Gaslight, Café Wha?, and the Bitter End.
Greenwich Village coffeehouse on West 4th Street where Bob Dylan performed; Robert Shelton's 1961 New York Times review of Dylan was written after a show there.
Annual folk festival in Newport, Rhode Island, founded 1959; Bob Dylan went electric there on July 25, 1965, marking the folk revival's symbolic end.
Civil rights anthem adapted from a gospel hymn; Pete Seeger and Guy Carawan taught it to SNCC activists; Joan Baez sang it at the 1963 March on Washington.
Bob Dylan song (1963) from The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan; became the folk revival's anthem; Peter, Paul and Mary's cover reached number two on the Hot 100.
Bob Dylan's second album (Columbia, May 1963); included 'Blowin' in the Wind,' 'A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall,' and 'Masters of War.'
Folk trio (Peter Yarrow, Paul Stookey, Mary Travers) who were the folk revival's most commercially successful group; covered Dylan's 'Blowin' in the Wind.'
Genre that emerged in 1965 blending folk melodies with electric instruments and rock rhythms; the Byrds' 'Mr. Tambourine Man' and Dylan's electric work defined it.
Los Angeles rock band who released an electric version of Dylan's 'Mr. Tambourine Man' in April 1965; the single reached number one.
Bob Dylan's electric performance at the Newport Folk Festival on July 25, 1965; parts of the audience booed; the moment symbolized the folk revival's end.

glossary.term: Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music
glossary.explain: Six-LP set (Folkways, 1952) of 78 rpm recordings (1927–1932) compiled by Harry Smith; became a sacred text for folk revivalists.
Folk music magazine founded in 1950 by Pete Seeger and others; became the folk community's journal.
1940s folk group (Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger, Lee Hays) that sang union songs and anti-fascist ballads; disbanded in 1943.
Blues and folk singer (1888–1949) who wrote 'Goodnight Irene'; the Weavers' cover reached number one in 1950.
Lead Belly song covered by the Weavers in 1950; reached number one on the Billboard chart and stayed there for thirteen weeks.
McCarthyera persecution of alleged Communists; Pete Seeger and the Weavers were blacklisted in 1952, ending their commercial careers.
Greenwich Village blues singer and Dylan's mentor; played ragtime guitar and Lead Belly covers; Dylan borrowed his arrangement of 'House of the Rising Sun.'
Gospel-trained singer (1930–2008) with a powerful voice; central figure in the Greenwich Village scene and the civil rights movement.
Folk singer (1931–) who traveled with Woody Guthrie and sang in Guthrie's style; performed in Greenwich Village.
Old-time string band (Mike Seeger, John Cohen, Tom Paley) that played Appalachian music with banjo, fiddle, and guitar.
New York Times music critic whose September 1961 review of Bob Dylan at Gerde's Folk City led to Dylan's Columbia Records contract.
Columbia Records producer who signed Bob Dylan in 1961; had previously signed Billie Holiday, Count Basie, and Aretha Franklin.
Mimeographed topical-song magazine founded February 1962 by Agnes 'Sis' Cunningham, Gordon Friesen, and Gil Turner; published Dylan's early songs.
Blues singer (1893–1966) whose 1920s recordings appeared on Harry Smith's Anthology; rediscovered in 1963 and performed at Newport.
Delta blues singer (1902–1988) rediscovered in the 1960s; his 1930s recordings influenced the folk revival.
Blues singer (1902–1969) rediscovered in 1964; his 1931 recordings appeared on reissue compilations.
August 28, 1963, civil rights march in Washington, D.C., with over 250,000 attendees; folk singers performed throughout the day.
Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, civil rights organization; activists sang 'We Shall Overcome' and other folk songs at sit-ins and marches.
SNCC activists (Rutha Mae Harris, Bernice Johnson Reagon, Cordell Reagon, Charles Neblett) who sang to raise funds and awareness for the civil rights movement.
Folk singer and Highlander Folk School staff member who taught 'We Shall Overcome' to SNCC activists in 1960.
Tennessee labor and civil rights education center where Zilphia Horton taught 'We Shall Overcome' to Pete Seeger.
Bob Dylan album (Columbia, January 1964) of protest and topical songs; title track became an anthem of generational change.
Topical songwriter (1940–1976) who wrote 'I Ain't Marching Anymore' and 'Draft Dodger Rag'; remained in the acoustic protest-song tradition.
Folk singer-songwriter (1937–) who wrote 'The Last Thing on My Mind' and 'Lyndon Johnson Told the Nation.'
Cree singer-songwriter (1941–) who wrote 'Universal Soldier,' an anti-war song covered by Donovan.
Classically trained singer (1939–) who recorded Dylan songs and traditional ballads with an operatic voice.
Canadian folk duo (Ian Tyson, Sylvia Fricker) who sang traditional and contemporary folk in the 1960s.
ABC television show (1963–1964) that brought folk music to living rooms nationwide but blacklisted Pete Seeger.
Bob Dylan album (August 1964) with personal and surreal songs ('My Back Pages,' 'Chimes of Freedom') rather than topical anthems.
Bob Dylan album (March 1965) with electric instruments on side one and acoustic songs on side two; included 'Subterranean Homesick Blues.'
Bob Dylan electric rock single (1965) with a promotional film; early music video.
Electric blues guitarist who played with Dylan at Newport 1965.
Organist who played with Dylan at Newport 1965 and on Highway 61 Revisited.
Bob Dylan electric rock album (September 1965); included 'Like a Rolling Stone,' which reached number two on the Hot 100.
Bob Dylan six-minute electric rock single (1965) that reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100.
Bob Dylan song; the Byrds' electric version (April 1965) reached number one, marking the birth of folk rock.
Folk duo (Paul Simon, Art Garfunkel); their 'The Sound of Silence' was overdubbed with electric instruments in 1965 and reached number one in 1966.
Simon & Garfunkel song recorded acoustically in 1964; producer Tom Wilson added electric instruments in 1965, and it reached number one.
Producer who worked with Dylan on Highway 61 Revisited and overdubbed Simon & Garfunkel's 'The Sound of Silence' with electric instruments.
Vocal group who sang folk harmonies with pop arrangements in the mid-1960s.
Folk rock band who played jug-band folk with electric guitars in the mid-1960s.
British folk singer who imitated Dylan and moved to psychedelic folk rock; covered Buffy Sainte-Marie's 'Universal Soldier.'
British folk singer (1915–1989) who wrote 'The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face' and 'Dirty Old Town'; led the British folk revival.
British folk scholar and singer (1908–1982) who collected and performed English folk songs.
British folk singer (1935–) who sang traditional ballads with minimal accompaniment.
British folk singer and guitarist (1941–) who taught Dylan 'Scarborough Fair' and 'Lord Franklin' in 1962.
Traditional English ballad; Martin Carthy taught it to Bob Dylan, who adapted it as 'Girl from the North Country'; Simon & Garfunkel recorded it in 1966.
British genre (mid-1950s) that played folk, blues, and country songs with acoustic guitars and homemade instruments; bridge between folk and rock.
British skiffle singer whose 'Rock Island Line' (1955) was a hit; influenced the Beatles and other British rock musicians.
Latin American folk movement (1960s–1970s) with explicitly political songs about social justice, indigenous rights, and resistance to dictatorships.
Chilean folk singer and songwriter (1917–1967) who collected traditional songs and wrote 'Gracias a la Vida'; key figure in nueva canción.
Chilean singer, theater director, and activist (1932–1973) who sang about land reform and worker rights; murdered by the Chilean military in 1973.
Argentine folk singer (1908–1992) who sang indigenous songs and wrote about rural life and social inequality.
Argentine folk singer (1935–2009) known as 'the voice of the voiceless Americas'; key figure in nueva canción.
Song about contemporary political or social issues; Phil Ochs, Tom Paxton, and early Bob Dylan wrote topical songs.
Artist who writes and performs their own songs; the folk revival established this as a legitimate role, influencing Joni Mitchell, Leonard Cohen, and 1970s folk.
Greenwich Village coffeehouse on MacDougal Street where Bob Dylan and others performed in the early 1960s.
Greenwich Village coffeehouse on MacDougal Street; Bob Dylan performed there in 1961.
Greenwich Village music club where folk singers performed in the 1960s.
Cambridge, Massachusetts, coffeehouse where Joan Baez sang before her 1959 Newport performance.
Label that released Joan Baez's albums and recorded rediscovered blues singers at Newport in the 1960s.
Independent label founded by Moses Asch that released Harry Smith's Anthology and Pete Seeger's albums.
Major label that released the Kingston Trio's 'Tom Dooley' in 1958.
Major label that signed Bob Dylan in 1961 and released his albums through the 1960s.
Informal folk music gathering where participants sing and play; the term was popularized in the 1940s and used for the 1963 TV show.
Central value of the folk revival; the belief that music should be rooted in tradition, sincere, and uncommercial; who got to define it was contested.
Gospel singer (1911–1972) who sang 'I Been 'Buked and I Been Scorned' at the 1963 March on Washington, before Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech.
1964–1966 wave of British rock bands (the Beatles, the Rolling Stones) that influenced Bob Dylan to go electric.
Guitar with twelve strings (six pairs) that produces a shimmering sound; the Byrds used a twelve-string electric guitar on 'Mr. Tambourine Man.'
Woody Guthrie song (1940) that became an American folk anthem; originally included verses critical of private property.
Traditional folk song about a New Orleans brothel; Dave Van Ronk's arrangement was borrowed by Bob Dylan and later by the Animals.
Member of the Freedom Singers and civil rights activist; later founded the a cappella group Sweet Honey in the Rock.
Song written by Pete Seeger and Lee Hays in 1949; Peter, Paul and Mary's 1962 version reached number ten on the Hot 100.
Jazz and folk festival promoter who organized the first Newport Folk Festival in 1959.
Canadian singer-songwriter (1943–) who emerged from the folk revival tradition and became a major 1970s artist.
Canadian singer-songwriter and poet (1934–2016) who emerged from the folk revival tradition.
